results.content:
Turn clicks into ready-made guides — as PDF, GIF, MP4, HTML, Markdown or a portrait video. All local, on your Mac.
StepGrab turns any workflow into a clean, numbered step-by-step guide — automatically. Start a recording, click through your process, and StepGrab captures a screenshot on every click, describes each action, and builds the guide for you.
StepGrab is a menu bar app: it sits quietly at the top of your Mac's menu bar, so a recording is always just one click away
100% offline. Your screen never leaves your Mac — no cloud, and no account required to start.
Features:
• Automatic click detection — a screenshot on every interaction
• Numbered step-by-step guides, generated as you work
• Smart action descriptions for every step
• Animated GIF export — quick, looping previews [...] • Animated GIF export — quick, looping previews
• Dynamic PDF guides (Pro) — professional documentation
• MP4 video export (Pro) — high-resolution guide videos
• Customizable design — colors, numbering styles, and layout
• Menu bar app — instant recording, stays out of your way
• Available in 7 languages
Perfect for support teams, onboarding, SOPs, training, and anyone who explains the same task twice.
Pricing:
• Free: up to 5 steps per recording
• Free account: 10 steps and 10 recordings
• Pro: unlimited steps, unlimited recordings, and all export formats — subscribe yearly, or pay once with a Lifetime license.
Everything is processed locally on your Mac.
Terms of Use & Privacy: [...] Thanks for the detailed feedback, and I'm sorry it didn't fit your workflow.A bit of the reasoning: on export, the annotations are rendered directly into the finished PDF, GIF or MP4 instead of staying as editable overlays. That was deliberate. The editable route, where you'd tweak them afterward in Apple's Preview, gets misaligned and messy fast, and the whole point of StepGrab is that you record once and walk away with a clean, finished guide, not another file to edit.On badges covering text: they're always placed in the area diagonally opposite the click, so they land in empty space rather than over what you just interacted with. A badge on critical text should be rare, and if you've hit a case where it happens, please send it over, that genuinely helps me fix it.The core of the app

# A Guidde alternative that stays on your Mac.

Quick answer: StepGrab is a native macOS app that captures a task once and turns it into an annotated screenshot guide entirely on your Mac, with no account and nothing uploaded. Guidde is a cloud-based AI platform that turns recordings into narrated videos for teams, with voiceover, translation, and helpdesk integrations. Choose StepGrab for fast, private, single-user guides on a Mac. Choose Guidde for team video documentation with AI narration. [...] StepGrab is a native macOS app that turns one recorded task into an annotated screenshot guide, entirely on your device, with no account and no upload. Guidde is a cloud platform built around AI-narrated video, aimed at teams that need shared workspaces, translation, and helpdesk integrations.

### Can StepGrab make videos like Guidde does?

StepGrab can export a guide as an animated GIF or MP4 on its Pro tier, but its core output is a cropped, annotated screenshot with a numbered arrow and a written step description. Guidde's core output is an AI-narrated video with voiceover, generated in the cloud.

For years my answer was the same ritual: take screenshots, crop them, draw arrows in Preview, paste it all into a document, send it off. Then three weeks later someone asks the same question, the app has updated, and half my screenshots are wrong.

StepGrab came out of six months of fixing that for myself. It lives in the Mac menu bar. You hit record, do the task once, and stop. Every click comes back as an annotated screenshot with an arrow on what you clicked and a step description written by a model running on your Mac. Export it as a GIF, a PDF or an MP4. Pro $2.99/mo, $12.99/yr, or $44.99 once. [...] There's a real constraint behind that one. To describe a click you need to know what was clicked, and on macOS that lives in the Accessibility API. I have shipped a build that used it, but approval for that entitlement is inconsistent enough that I can't put a core feature on top of it. So I reconstruct from OCR and cursor position instead. When a control carries visible text that works well. When it's an unlabelled toolbar icon it doesn't, and that layer is still very much in development. The image foundation model coming in macOS 27 should close most of the gap, and until then I'm grateful for any ideas.
